subject: mathematics
question_text: If A + B + C = 180°, then show that sin2A + sin2B + sin2C = 4 sinA sinB sinC.

mark_split.label: Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula
Apply the product formula and conclude

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Junior Inter Maths-1A (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.39 — LAQ chapter 5 T-Ratios upto Transformations, answer 26.1. Printed appearances: none — this answer carries no year tag, but its twin 26.2 on the same page carries AP 17 and TS 16. The book pairs it with 26.2 and notes "What a pairing! So easy, so similar" — the two differ only in sine against cosine. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S — no [N Marks] tags are printed anywhere in this chapter (its pages are set two questions to a page in two columns, which takes the margin those tags would occupy). The 1+2+2+1+1 above follows the shape of the split the same book DOES print for LAQ answer 23 on book p.37, weighting the two substantial transformations against the set-up and the finish. The SAME split and the SAME step ids are used on all eight answers in this chapter, deliberately: they are ONE method over different identities — pair two terms, use the angle condition, factor, finish with a product formula. A student who learns that arc once can attempt any of them. The book's chapter header carries ★★ and reads '7 Marks'; that star is the CHAPTER's rank, not this question's. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it. Paper position: Maths-1A Section C runs Q18-Q24 at 7 marks each, answer any 5 of 7; Q23 is the Transformations slot and is ALWAYS a question of this kind. Re-cut to the 8-mark Section-C form of the 2026-27 pattern (TGBIE model paper w.e.f. 2026-27): the extra mark goes to Pair two terms with a sum-to-product formula.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this identity — say the four moves in order, and where the angle condition gets used.

steps.label: State the angle condition
steps.margin_note: First mark. The angle condition is the ONLY thing that makes this an identity rather than a false statement, so it is written before any transformation.
steps.memory_tip: A + B = 180° − C. This condition is the ONLY thing making the statement true, so write it first.

recall.must_convey: That the angle condition is written down first, in the form the proof will actually use.
accept: write the angle condition first in the form the proof needs
state the given condition and rearrange it
note the angle sum before starting the transformation
modata angle condition rasi, kavalsina form lo pettali
write down the condition on the angles

steps.why: Without the condition the statement is simply false, so it is not preamble — it is the hypothesis the whole proof leans on, and it is used at least twice below.
common_mistakes: Starting the transformation before writing the condition.
Writing the condition but never rearranging it into a usable form.

steps.label: Pair two terms
steps.margin_note: Three of the eight marks. Three terms will not factorise as they stand, so two of them are combined into a product first. Quote the formula in brackets — the formulas are what the examiner marks.
steps.memory_tip: Pair sin2A with sin2B, and expand sin2C as 2 sinC cosC so both terms carry sin C.

recall.must_convey: That the first TWO terms are paired with the sin C + sin D formula, and the third is expanded by sin 2θ = 2 sinθ cosθ.
accept: pair the first two with the sin C plus sin D formula and expand sin two C as two sin C cos C
apply sum to product on sin two A plus sin two B and double angle on the third
combine two of the terms and expand the other one
modati rendu terms ni sum to product cheyyali, moodava term double angle
use sinC plus sinD on the first pair

steps.why: Three terms cannot be factorised as they stand. Pairing two of them produces a common factor that the third can then join.
common_mistakes: Trying to expand all three terms at once.
Pairing the wrong two terms, which leaves nothing in common.

steps.label: Use the condition
steps.margin_note: Two more marks. This is where the angle condition earns its place: it converts an expression in A and B into one in C, so that every term shares a factor.
steps.memory_tip: sin(180° − C) = +sin C — a PLUS here, unlike the cosine version.

recall.must_convey: That A + B is replaced by 180° − C, and sin(180° − C) simplifies to sin C — which is what makes the two terms share a factor.
accept: replace A plus B by one eighty minus C and sin of one eighty minus C is sin C
use the angle condition so both terms carry sin C
substitute the angle sum so sin A plus B becomes sin C
A plus B ni one eighty minus C ga marchi, sin C vasthundi
convert using the supplementary angle

steps.why: sin(180° − θ) = sin θ is what turns sin(A+B) into sin C. Without the angle condition the two terms would never share a factor.
common_mistakes: Writing sin(180° − C) = −sin C, which is the cosine rule not the sine one.
Forgetting to use the condition at all.

steps.label: Take the common factor out
steps.margin_note: Seventh mark. The common factor comes out, and the condition is used a SECOND time inside the bracket so that both bracket terms are the same kind of function.
steps.memory_tip: Take 2 sinC out, then use cos(180° − θ) = −cos θ so the bracket becomes a difference.

recall.must_convey: That 2 sin C is taken out as a common factor, and that cos C is rewritten as −cos(A+B) using the angle condition a second time.
accept: take two sin C common then rewrite cos C as minus cos A plus B
factor out two sin C and convert the cosine using the angle sum again
the common factor comes out and cos C becomes minus cos of A plus B
two sin C common teesi, cos C ni minus cos A plus B ga marchali
use the condition a second time on the cosine

steps.why: The angle condition is used TWICE — once on the sine and once on the cosine. Missing the second use leaves a bracket that will not collapse.
common_mistakes: Writing cos(180° − θ) = +cos θ and losing the minus.
Taking out sin C instead of 2 sin C.

steps.label: Apply the product formula
steps.margin_note: Last mark. One more sum-or-difference formula turns the bracket into a product, and the identity closes. Write "= R.H.S" so the examiner can see it landed.
steps.memory_tip: cos(A−B) − cos(A+B) = 2 sinA sinB, giving the 4 in the answer.

recall.must_convey: That cos(A−B) − cos(A+B) = 2 sinA sinB is applied, giving 4 sinA sinB sinC.
accept: use cos A minus B minus cos A plus B equals two sin A sin B to get four sin A sin B sin C
the bracket becomes two sin A sin B so the answer is four sin A sin B sin C
apply the product formula to finish
cos A minus B minus cos A plus B equals two sin A sin B, so four sin A sin B sin C
the last formula gives four sin A sin B sin C
heard_as: four sin A sin B sin C

steps.why: The difference of two cosines is a product of two sines. That single formula turns the bracket into the two factors the answer needs.
common_mistakes: Using cos(A+B) − cos(A−B), which gives the wrong sign.
Stopping at the bracket without applying the formula.

insider_note: Pair the first two into 2sin(A+B)cos(A−B), then sin(180° − C) = sinC. The bracket becomes cos(A−B) − cos(A+B) = 2 sinA sinB, and that minus sign is essential.
